summary: Defines an extension to SMTP that lets a message carry a priority label so mail servers along its path can handle it preferentially. It is a standards-track specification, described as giving messages transfer priorities, and is aimed at environments where some mail must move ahead of other mail.

eli5.summary: Like a line at the airport where some people get a fast lane, this lets important emails carry a tag that says please let me through first.

subtitle: A way for a mail message to carry a priority from -9 to 9 so busy servers can move urgent mail first.

tldr.problem: When bandwidth, round trip time, storage or processing is limited, some messages matter more than others, but plain SMTP gives a server no way to know which ones to relay first.
tldr.mechanism: The MT-PRIORITY SMTP extension adds one optional parameter to the MAIL FROM command carrying a whole number from -9 to 9. Servers pass it on hop by hop and send higher-priority messages first.
tldr.outcome: It is best effort only: there is no guarantee that a higher-priority message arrives before a lower-priority one, and servers must not accept raised priorities from untrusted senders.

today: RFC 6710 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the definition of the MT-PRIORITY SMTP extension.

sections.title: Why Mail Needs Priorities
sections.content:
Where resources for switching or transferring messages are constrained (bandwidth, round trip time, transition storage or processing capability), it is desirable to give some messages preferential handling according to a labeled priority. The RFC points to emergencies for first responders, and to military and aviation messaging, where delay can have serious consequences.

The extension helps most on networks with limited bandwidth or long round trip times, such as satellite or high-frequency radio links, and when an MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) queue builds up because mail arrives faster than it leaves. When neither condition holds, the RFC says the extension will not give any user better service.

The service is best effort. For two messages with priorities M and N where M is greater than N, submitted at the same time, the extension does not promise that the higher-priority one arrives first.
sections.eli5: If a road is jammed, an ambulance gets to go first. This gives urgent emails a way to say they are the ambulance, but it cannot promise they will always win.

sections.title: The MT-PRIORITY Extension
sections.content:
The extension is called Priority Message Handling. A server announces it with the EHLO keyword MT-PRIORITY. No new SMTP verbs are added. Instead, an optional MT-PRIORITY parameter is added to the MAIL FROM command. Its value is a decimal integer from -9 to 9 inclusive, and higher numbers mean higher priority. By default each message has priority 0.

The EHLO keyword may carry an optional parameter naming the Priority Assignment Policy the server uses. If the parameter is absent, the server is unwilling to disclose its policy, and clients may still use the extension. The maximum length of a MAIL FROM line grows by 15 octets to make room. The extension is valid for message submission and for LMTP.

One priority applies to all recipients of the same message, which keeps implementations simpler.
sections.eli5: The server shows a sign saying it understands priority tags. A sender then writes a number from -9 to 9 on the envelope, and bigger numbers mean more urgent.

sections.title: How Servers Handle and Relay Priorities
sections.content:
A receiving server returns an error such as 501 syntax error in parameter (enhanced code 5.5.2) if a priority value is malformed or if a MAIL FROM carries more than one MT-PRIORITY parameter. It SHOULD log the received value and SHOULD include a PRIORITY clause in the Received header field it adds.

When relaying to a server that supports the extension, the MTA MUST include an MT-PRIORITY parameter with the priority it determined, which may differ from what it received because of site policy. When relaying to a server without the extension, it simply omits the parameter. Mailing lists and aliases SHOULD keep the priority for every expanded address.

A server may change a message's priority to enforce site policy. If it does, it SHOULD answer with the X.3.6 enhanced status code, followed by the new priority and an explanation. A submission server may also reject a message with a 450 or 550 reply and the X.7.15 code when the priority is below the lowest it currently accepts. Delivery reports SHOULD use the priority of the message they report on, but relayed delivery reports get no special treatment, because boosting them would let untrusted systems inject fake high-priority notices.
sections.eli5: Each post office reads the number, keeps it on the parcel, and passes it along. A post office that does not know about numbers just passes the parcel without one.

sections.title: Expedited Transfer and Priority Levels
sections.content:
Priority changes the order in which a client sends messages to a server. A client with several messages to send sends higher-priority ones first, and may use shorter retry intervals and shorter timeouts before a non-delivery report for them. Within one priority level the MTA uses its normal ordering algorithm.

A server does not have to treat all 19 values as separate levels, but it MUST implement every level its Priority Assignment Policy defines. A value it does not support is rounded up to the next higher supported level, or to the highest supported level. Whatever it does internally, it MUST pass on the priority it determined when relaying or delivering over LMTP.

A policy may also cap message size by priority. A server that refuses a message as too big for its priority SHOULD use a 552 reply with the X.7.16 code. If the server also supports the SIZE extension, a client can send both SIZE= and MT-PRIORITY= so the server can refuse early instead of after the transfer. The extension can also be combined with DELIVERBY, which provides timely delivery, but the two are not required to be implemented together.
sections.eli5: When you have a stack of letters to send, you mail the urgent ones first. If the post office only has a few lanes, a number between two lanes goes to the faster one.

sections.title: Syntax and a Worked Example
sections.content:
The formal syntax uses ABNF. A priority value is an optional minus sign followed by a digit 1 to 9, or the single digit 0. The EHLO line is MT-PRIORITY, optionally followed by a space and a policy name of 1 to 20 letters, digits, hyphens, underscores or dots. The Received clause is PRIORITY followed by the value.

In the RFC's example, a mail client connects to a submission server that advertises 250 MT-PRIORITY MIXER, authenticates, and sends MAIL FROM with MT-PRIORITY=3. The server accepts it. The example also uses STARTTLS, DELIVERBY and DSN, though none of those is required.
sections.eli5: The rules say exactly how to write the number and the policy name so every server reads them the same way. The example shows a sender writing a 3 and the server saying fine.

sections.title: Deployment and Priority Assignment Policies
sections.content:
If a domain has several MX servers, the RFC strongly advises that all of them support the extension and handle priorities identically. Otherwise, none should support it, or delivery speed and even rejections will differ unpredictably during failures.

Senders in one environment need to use priority values by roughly the same criteria, so that one sender's 3 does not mean another's 5. A Priority Assignment Policy, documented for the environment, fixes this. The default policy is MIXER. The RFC also defines STANAG4406 (military messaging) and NSEP (national security and emergency preparedness). Every MSA, MTA and MDA in an administrative domain has to use the same policy, and cooperating domains need compatible ones, or a high-priority fake delivery report could be injected.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to agree what a 5 means, like all the classrooms using the same rules for who goes first in the lunch line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Submission servers ought to accept priorities only from users who are authenticated and authorized in some way the server accepts, and MTAs likewise for senders. A server can cap the maximum priority a group may request and can override the value a client set.

The server MUST NOT allow positive priorities from untrusted or unauthorized sources, though it MAY let such a source lower its own priority. Without this enforcement, a server could suffer a denial-of-service attack in which malicious clients always ask for priority 9.
sections.eli5: Only people with a real pass should get the fast lane. If everyone could just say they are most important, the fast lane would jam up.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added MT-PRIORITY to the SMTP Service Extensions registry, and the PRIORITY clause to the Additional-registered-clauses sub-registry for Received headers. It also added three enhanced status codes and created a new registry for Priority Assignment Policies, with Specification Required registration. The initial entries are MIXER (the default), STANAG4406 and NSEP.

A policy registration must name the policy in 1 to 20 US-ASCII characters and list the supported priority levels. It must also cover retry and expiration timeouts, maximum message sizes, and any authentication requirements, and it may not redefine the -9 to 9 range.
sections.eli5: A public notebook records the new keyword, the new error codes, and the list of rule books that servers may announce.

items.label: Priority Level is too low
items.desc: The priority is below the lowest the server currently accepts; may be temporary.

items.label: Message is too big for the specified priority
items.desc: Used with a 552 reply when the message exceeds the size allowed for its priority.

items.label: Requested priority was changed
items.desc: Message accepted but the requested priority was not honored; text gives the new priority.
